hook.text: Aspirin is made by chemistry — insulin is made by living cells. That difference defines biopharmaceuticals.

buildup.text: Traditional drugs are small molecules synthesized chemically — biologics are large proteins grown in cells.

discovery.text: Biologics include antibodies, hormones, enzymes, and vaccines — they target disease with molecular precision.

twist.text: Biologics cannot be taken as pills — their protein structures would be destroyed by stomach acid.

climax.text: Biopharmaceuticals now account for over 40% of drug revenue — and the share keeps growing every year.

punchline.text: Living cells make the medicine — biology beats chemistry for complex diseases.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between biopharmaceuticals and traditional drugs?
options: Biopharmaceuticals are always cheaper to produce
Biopharmaceuticals are large proteins produced by living cells, not chemical synthesis
Traditional drugs cannot treat chronic diseases

hook.text: Before 1982, diabetics injected pig or cow insulin — it sometimes caused allergic reactions. Then came Humulin.

buildup.text: Genentech inserted the human insulin gene into E. coli bacteria — the microbes became tiny insulin factories.

discovery.text: Humulin was the first recombinant drug approved by the FDA — identical to human insulin, made by bacteria.

twist.text: Modern insulin analogs are engineered beyond human — lispro acts faster, glargine lasts longer. Better than nature.

climax.text: Over 100 million people depend on recombinant insulin — the first biopharmaceutical saved an entire industry.

punchline.text: Bacteria make human insulin — biotech's first drug, still saving lives.

quiz.question: What made Humulin historically significant?
options: It was the first insulin that could be taken orally
It was the first recombinant DNA drug approved by the FDA
It was extracted from a new animal source

hook.text: Growth hormone was once harvested from cadaver pituitary glands — some batches transmitted fatal brain disease.

buildup.text: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease from contaminated hormone killed over 200 children — the supply had to change.

discovery.text: Recombinant human growth hormone replaced cadaver sources in 1985 — E. coli produced unlimited, safe supply.

twist.text: Safe supply led to broader use — now prescribed for Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, and adult deficiency.

climax.text: The transition from cadaver to recombinant happened in just three years — biotech solved a deadly safety crisis.

punchline.text: From cadavers to bacteria — recombinant tech ended a tragedy.

quiz.question: Why was cadaver-derived growth hormone replaced?
options: It was too expensive to extract from pituitary glands
Some batches transmitted Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a fatal brain disorder
It caused allergic reactions in all patients

hook.text: EPO tells your body to make more red blood cells — for kidney patients, it ended decades of severe anemia.

buildup.text: Healthy kidneys produce EPO naturally — but damaged kidneys cannot, leaving patients chronically exhausted.

discovery.text: Recombinant EPO is made in CHO cells — Chinese hamster ovary cells add the sugar coatings the protein needs.

twist.text: Athletes abused EPO for blood doping — Lance Armstrong's downfall was partly due to illegal EPO use.

climax.text: EPO remains one of the most successful biologics ever — treating millions of dialysis patients worldwide.

punchline.text: A kidney hormone from hamster cells — saving patients, tempting cheaters.

quiz.question: Why is EPO produced in CHO cells rather than bacteria?
options: CHO cells grow faster than bacteria
CHO cells add sugar modifications that the protein requires to function properly
Bacteria cannot express any mammalian genes

hook.text: Your cells release interferons when viruses attack — these signaling proteins alert the neighborhood to danger.

buildup.text: Interferon-alpha activates immune cells against viruses — it was the first biologic for hepatitis B and C.

discovery.text: Interferon-beta slows multiple sclerosis — reducing relapse rates by about 30% in clinical trials.

twist.text: PEGylation attaches polymer chains to interferon — extending its half-life from hours to days in the body.

climax.text: Recombinant interferons replaced blood-derived versions — safer, cheaper, and available in unlimited quantities.

punchline.text: The body's alarm signal, bottled — interferons fight viruses and disease.

quiz.question: What does PEGylation do to interferon drugs?
options: It makes them small enough to cross the blood-brain barrier
It attaches polymer chains that extend the drug's duration in the body
It changes the interferon from a protein into a small molecule

hook.text: Gaucher disease patients lack one enzyme — their cells fill with undigested fat, swelling liver and spleen.

buildup.text: Ceredase was the first enzyme replacement — purified from human placentas. It took 20,000 placentas per patient per year.

discovery.text: Cerezyme replaced it — recombinant glucocerebrosidase from CHO cells, unlimited supply without human tissue.

twist.text: ERT now treats Fabry, Pompe, and MPS disorders — but costs over $200,000 per patient per year.

climax.text: These drugs transformed fatal childhood diseases into manageable conditions — price is the remaining barrier.

punchline.text: Replace what the body cannot make — enzyme therapy is liquid rescue.

quiz.question: Why is enzyme replacement therapy so expensive?
options: The enzymes must be imported from only one country
Production requires complex mammalian cell culture and patient populations are very small
The enzymes degrade immediately and need continuous infusion

hook.text: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock onto targets — monoclonal antibodies are armies of identical copies.

buildup.text: Each monoclonal antibody recognizes one specific epitope — a tiny patch on a protein surface.

discovery.text: Binding the target can block a receptor, flag a cell for destruction, or neutralize a toxin.

twist.text: The first monoclonals were mouse antibodies — human immune systems attacked them. Humanization solved this.

climax.text: Over 100 monoclonal antibodies are now approved — treating cancer, autoimmune disease, and infections.

punchline.text: One target, one antibody — precision medicine in protein form.

quiz.question: Why did early mouse monoclonal antibodies need to be humanized?
options: Mouse antibodies were too large to inject into humans
The human immune system recognized mouse proteins as foreign and attacked them
Mouse antibodies could not bind human disease targets

hook.text: B cells make antibodies but die quickly in culture — cancer cells are immortal but make no useful antibodies.

buildup.text: Köhler and Milstein fused them — creating hybridomas that are both immortal and antibody-producing.

discovery.text: HAT selection medium kills unfused cells — only the hybrid survives, producing unlimited monoclonal antibodies.

twist.text: The inventors did not patent it — they shared the technology freely. It won them the 1984 Nobel Prize.

climax.text: Hybridoma technology launched a multibillion-dollar industry — from research reagents to life-saving drugs.

punchline.text: Fuse a B cell with a cancer cell — get an immortal antibody factory.

quiz.question: What is a hybridoma?
options: A type of virus used to deliver antibodies
A fusion of an antibody-producing B cell and an immortal cancer cell
A genetically modified bacterium that secretes antibodies

hook.text: Chemotherapy poisons all dividing cells — what if you could deliver the poison only to cancer cells?

buildup.text: Antibody-drug conjugates link a toxic payload to an antibody — the antibody finds the tumor, the drug kills it.

discovery.text: A chemical linker holds the payload — it breaks only inside the cancer cell, releasing the poison precisely.

twist.text: Early ADCs failed because linkers broke too early — releasing toxin in the bloodstream. Stable linkers fixed this.

climax.text: Enhertu treats breast cancer with HER2 — its bystander effect kills even neighboring cancer cells that lack the target.

punchline.text: A guided missile with a warhead — ADCs deliver chemo to the doorstep.

quiz.question: How do antibody-drug conjugates reduce chemotherapy side effects?
options: They use a less toxic form of chemotherapy drug
The antibody delivers the toxic payload specifically to cancer cells, sparing healthy tissue
They prevent the drug from entering the bloodstream entirely

hook.text: Cancer hides from your immune system by pressing the brakes — checkpoint inhibitors release those brakes.

buildup.text: PD-1 on T cells acts as an off switch — cancer cells display PD-L1 to silence the attack.

discovery.text: Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1 — T cells wake up and attack tumors they previously ignored.

twist.text: Not all cancers respond — only tumors with many mutations tend to benefit from checkpoint therapy.

climax.text: James Allison and Tasuku Honjo won the 2018 Nobel Prize — their discovery launched modern immunotherapy.

punchline.text: Release the brakes on immunity — and let your body fight the cancer.

quiz.question: How does PD-L1 on cancer cells help tumors evade the immune system?
options: It makes cancer cells invisible to all immune cells
It binds PD-1 on T cells, sending an off signal that prevents attack
It directly kills T cells that approach the tumor

hook.text: Normal antibodies have two identical arms — bispecific antibodies have two different arms, grabbing two different targets.

buildup.text: One arm binds a cancer cell, the other grabs a T cell — physically dragging the killer to the target.

discovery.text: Blinatumomab treats leukemia by connecting T cells to CD19 on cancer cells — a molecular matchmaker.

twist.text: Engineering two different arms into one protein is complex — asymmetric assembly causes manufacturing headaches.

climax.text: Over 200 bispecifics are in clinical trials — the format explosion is reshaping cancer treatment strategies.

punchline.text: Two targets, one drug — bispecifics bridge immunity to disease.

quiz.question: How do bispecific antibodies help treat cancer?
options: They deliver chemotherapy drugs directly into tumor cells
One arm binds a cancer cell while the other recruits an immune cell to attack it
They block two growth signals on the same cancer cell

hook.text: Camels and llamas make antibodies with no light chains — just a single heavy chain. They are tiny and tough.

buildup.text: The antigen-binding domain is just 15 kDa — one-tenth the size of a regular antibody. It is called a nanobody.

discovery.text: Nanobodies penetrate tissues that full antibodies cannot reach — including solid tumors and the blood-brain barrier.

twist.text: They survive boiling and stomach acid — opening the door to oral and inhaled biologic drugs.

climax.text: Cablivi, the first approved nanobody, treats blood clotting disorders — camelid biology becomes human medicine.

punchline.text: From llama blood to human drugs — nanobodies are small but mighty.

quiz.question: What makes nanobodies different from conventional antibodies?
options: They are synthetic chemicals, not proteins
They are ten times smaller, more stable, and derived from camelid heavy-chain-only antibodies
They can only be used in veterinary medicine

hook.text: mRNA vaccines teach your cells to make a viral protein — your immune system then learns to attack it.

buildup.text: Lipid nanoparticles deliver the mRNA into cells — the mRNA instructs ribosomes to build the spike protein.

discovery.text: The immune system sees the spike protein as foreign — B cells make antibodies, T cells learn to kill infected cells.

twist.text: mRNA degrades in days — no permanent genetic change occurs. The instructions vanish after the job is done.

climax.text: Pfizer and Moderna vaccines were designed in days and tested in months — mRNA slashed vaccine development time.

punchline.text: Send the recipe, not the virus — mRNA vaccines teach immunity from instructions.

quiz.question: Why do mRNA vaccines not alter your DNA?
options: They contain a special enzyme that protects DNA
mRNA works in the cytoplasm and degrades within days without entering the nucleus
The lipid nanoparticle prevents mRNA from reaching chromosomes

hook.text: Why inject a whole virus when one protein is enough? Subunit vaccines use just the piece that matters.

buildup.text: The hepatitis B vaccine was the first recombinant vaccine — yeast cells produce the surface antigen protein.

discovery.text: Novavax's COVID vaccine uses spike proteins grown in insect cells — no virus, no mRNA, just the purified protein.

twist.text: Pure proteins are weak immunogens alone — adjuvants like aluminum salts or saponins boost the immune response.

climax.text: Shingrix uses a recombinant glycoprotein with AS01B adjuvant — over 90% effective even in elderly patients.

punchline.text: One protein plus an adjuvant — subunit vaccines are safe and precise.

quiz.question: Why do subunit vaccines need adjuvants?
options: Adjuvants stabilize the protein during storage
Purified proteins alone provoke a weak immune response that adjuvants amplify
Adjuvants convert the protein into mRNA for better delivery

hook.text: Use a harmless virus to carry genes from a dangerous one — the body mounts a defense without facing the real threat.

buildup.text: AstraZeneca's COVID vaccine uses a chimpanzee adenovirus carrying the spike gene — the vector cannot replicate.

discovery.text: J&J used human adenovirus 26 — a single dose induced strong immunity because the vector triggers innate responses too.

twist.text: Pre-existing immunity to the vector can blunt the vaccine — people who had that adenovirus before respond less.

climax.text: The Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV uses a livestock virus carrying Ebola glycoprotein — 100% effective in ring vaccination trials.

punchline.text: A tame virus carrying enemy intel — viral vectors train immunity safely.

quiz.question: What is a challenge of using human adenovirus as a vaccine vector?
options: Human adenoviruses are too large to carry vaccine genes
Pre-existing immunity to the vector can reduce vaccine effectiveness
Adenoviruses always integrate into the genome permanently

hook.text: Can you vaccinate against cancer? Neoantigen vaccines teach your immune system to hunt your specific tumor.

buildup.text: Sequence the tumor's DNA, find mutations unique to it, and design an mRNA vaccine encoding those neoantigens.

discovery.text: Moderna's personalized cancer vaccine mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda cut melanoma recurrence by 44% in a Phase 2 trial.

twist.text: Every patient gets a different vaccine — manufacturing a unique drug per person upends traditional pharma economics.

climax.text: HPV vaccines prevent cervical cancer by stopping the virus — Gardasil prevents over 90% of HPV-related cancers.

punchline.text: Prevent or attack — cancer vaccines work both ways.

quiz.question: How are personalized cancer vaccines designed?
options: They use a standard protein found in all cancers
Tumor DNA is sequenced to find unique mutations, then a vaccine encoding those neoantigens is made
They are made from weakened cancer cells injected back into the patient

hook.text: Cytokines are the immune system's text messages — amplifying, calming, or redirecting immune responses.

buildup.text: IL-2 stimulates T cell growth — high-dose IL-2 was one of the first immunotherapies for metastatic melanoma.

discovery.text: TNF blockers like infliximab calm overactive immunity — transforming treatment for rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's.

twist.text: Cytokine storms kill — COVID deaths were partly caused by runaway IL-6 and TNF. Too much immune signaling is fatal.

climax.text: Engineered cytokines with extended half-lives and reduced toxicity are entering trials — precision immune tuning.

punchline.text: Boost or silence the immune signal — cytokines are the volume knob.

quiz.question: What is a cytokine storm?
options: A rapid increase in antibody production during vaccination
A dangerous overproduction of immune signaling molecules that can damage organs
The normal immune response to bacterial infections

hook.text: Most vaccines prevent disease — therapeutic vaccines treat diseases you already have. They retrain your immunity.

buildup.text: Sipuleucel-T treats prostate cancer — patient's own immune cells are exposed to a tumor antigen and reinfused.

discovery.text: Therapeutic hepatitis B vaccines aim to cure chronic infection — awakening exhausted T cells that ignore the virus.

twist.text: The immune system actively suppresses responses to chronic infections — breaking tolerance is the hardest challenge.

climax.text: Alzheimer's vaccines targeting amyloid plaques entered trials — immunotherapy expanding beyond infectious disease.

punchline.text: Not prevention but cure — therapeutic vaccines fight what is already there.

quiz.question: What makes therapeutic vaccines different from preventive vaccines?
options: They use stronger adjuvants than preventive vaccines
They treat existing diseases by reactivating the immune response against them
They prevent diseases from spreading to other people

hook.text: Chinese hamster ovary cells produce over 70% of all biopharmaceuticals — the unsung heroes of modern medicine.

buildup.text: CHO cells grow in suspension culture — massive stainless-steel bioreactors hold up to 20,000 liters.

discovery.text: CHO cells fold human proteins correctly and add proper sugar chains — bacteria cannot do this.

twist.text: Developing a stable CHO cell line takes 6 to 12 months — finding the best producer among millions of clones.

climax.text: Modern CHO cells produce over 10 grams of antibody per liter — a 100-fold improvement in 30 years.

punchline.text: Tiny hamster cells in giant tanks — the factory behind most biologics.

quiz.question: Why are CHO cells preferred over bacteria for producing most biopharmaceuticals?
options: CHO cells grow faster than any bacterial strain
CHO cells correctly fold proteins and add sugar modifications that bacteria cannot
Bacteria are too dangerous to use in pharmaceutical manufacturing

hook.text: Growing the protein is half the battle — purifying it from the cell soup is the other half. That is downstream.

buildup.text: Protein A chromatography captures antibodies from culture broth — like a magnet for immunoglobulins.

discovery.text: Ion exchange and size exclusion chromatography remove remaining impurities — achieving over 99% purity.

twist.text: Downstream processing accounts for up to 80% of manufacturing cost — purification is more expensive than production.

climax.text: Continuous chromatography systems run nonstop — cutting processing time and cost by 30% or more.

punchline.text: Grow it, catch it, clean it — downstream makes medicine from mess.

quiz.question: Why is downstream processing the most expensive step in biologic manufacturing?
options: The chemicals used are extremely rare and costly
Multiple purification steps with expensive chromatography equipment are needed to achieve high purity
Proteins are damaged during purification and must be regrown

hook.text: A single misfolded protein can kill — quality control in biologic manufacturing is a matter of life and death.

buildup.text: Mass spectrometry confirms the protein's exact mass and amino acid sequence — every batch is verified.

discovery.text: Glycan profiling ensures sugar modifications are consistent — even small changes affect drug safety and efficacy.

twist.text: Aggregation is the silent killer — clumped proteins trigger immune reactions. Size exclusion catches aggregates.

climax.text: Process analytical technology monitors quality in real time — catching problems during production, not after.

punchline.text: Test everything, trust nothing — QC keeps biologics safe.

quiz.question: Why is protein aggregation a safety concern in biologics?
options: Aggregated proteins are always inactive and waste money
Clumped proteins can trigger dangerous immune reactions in patients
Aggregation makes proteins too large to inject

hook.text: Generic drugs are identical copies — biosimilars are highly similar but never exactly the same. Biology is messy.

buildup.text: Biologics are too complex to copy perfectly — different cell lines produce slightly different glycosylation patterns.

discovery.text: Biosimilar approval requires analytical, functional, and clinical comparisons — proving equivalence is expensive.

twist.text: Biosimilars are 15 to 40% cheaper than originals — not the 90% discount of generic small molecules.

climax.text: Humira biosimilars finally launched in 2023 — breaking the best-selling drug's $20 billion annual monopoly.

punchline.text: Similar but not identical — biosimilars bring biologic prices down, not to the floor.

quiz.question: Why can't biosimilars be exact copies of the original biologic?
options: Patent law prevents exact replication of biologic drugs
Different cell lines and processes produce proteins with slight structural differences
Biosimilar manufacturers deliberately alter the protein to avoid lawsuits

hook.text: Biologics are proteins — leave them warm and they unfold, aggregate, or degrade. The cold chain keeps them alive.

buildup.text: Most antibodies require 2 to 8°C storage — mRNA vaccines initially needed minus 70°C with dry ice shipping.

discovery.text: Lyophilization freeze-dries proteins into powder — stable at room temperature for months, reconstituted before use.

twist.text: Cold chain failures destroy $35 billion in drugs annually — temperature excursions are a global health problem.

climax.text: Thermostable formulations with trehalose sugars protect proteins without refrigeration — crucial for remote clinics.

punchline.text: Keep it cold or lose the cure — stability is the last mile of biologics.

quiz.question: How does lyophilization improve biologic drug stability?
options: It converts proteins into small molecules that resist heat
Freeze-drying removes water, creating a stable powder that can be stored without refrigeration
It permanently changes the protein structure to tolerate higher temperatures

hook.text: Stainless steel bioreactors cost millions and take months to clean — disposable plastic bags changed the game.

buildup.text: Single-use bioreactors come pre-sterilized — no cleaning validation, no cross-contamination between batches.

discovery.text: Flexible manufacturing lets companies switch products in days — critical for personalized medicine and pandemics.

twist.text: Plastic waste is the downside — thousands of bags per year go to landfill. The industry is exploring recycling.

climax.text: Single-use systems now go up to 6,000 liters — large enough for commercial antibody production.

punchline.text: Use it once and toss it — disposable bioreactors trade waste for speed.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of single-use bioreactors over stainless steel?
options: They produce higher yields of protein per liter
They eliminate cleaning validation and allow rapid changeover between products
They are more environmentally friendly than stainless steel

hook.text: Zolgensma costs $2.1 million per dose — it is a one-time gene therapy that saves babies from fatal paralysis.

buildup.text: An AAV vector delivers a working copy of the SMN1 gene — motor neurons start producing the survival protein.

discovery.text: Babies treated before symptoms appear develop almost normally — early treatment is the key to maximum benefit.

twist.text: Manufacturing AAV at scale is a bottleneck — each dose requires trillions of viral particles, produced in huge batches.

climax.text: Over 20 gene therapy products are approved worldwide — a new class of biologics is becoming mainstream medicine.

punchline.text: One dose, one gene, one cure — gene therapy biologics rewrite the rules.

quiz.question: Why must Zolgensma be given early in a baby's life?
options: The AAV vector only works in immature immune systems
Motor neurons die progressively, so early treatment preserves more neurons for normal development
The gene only functions during the first year of life

hook.text: mRNA is not just for vaccines — Onpattro uses RNA interference to silence a disease gene in the liver.

buildup.text: Small interfering RNA binds messenger RNA and triggers its destruction — no protein is made from the silenced gene.

discovery.text: Onpattro treats hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis — silencing the faulty TTR gene stops toxic protein buildup.

twist.text: Antisense oligonucleotides work differently — they bind pre-mRNA to modify splicing or block translation.

climax.text: Inclisiran lowers cholesterol with two injections per year — siRNA against PCSK9 lasts for months per dose.

punchline.text: Silence the gene, stop the disease — RNA drugs rewrite pharmacology.

quiz.question: How does RNA interference silence a gene?
options: It edits the DNA sequence to remove the gene permanently
Small interfering RNA binds and triggers destruction of the target messenger RNA
It blocks ribosomes from attaching to any messenger RNA

hook.text: Living cells as medicine — not a molecule in a vial but billions of cells infused into the patient.

buildup.text: Mesenchymal stem cells dampen inflammation — clinical trials target graft-versus-host disease and osteoarthritis.

discovery.text: iPSC-derived cells could provide unlimited supply — one donor's cells reprogrammed to treat thousands of patients.

twist.text: Living drugs are unpredictable — cells can migrate, multiply, or change behavior inside the patient.

climax.text: Allogeneic off-the-shelf cell therapies avoid patient-specific manufacturing — freezer-ready doses for immediate use.

punchline.text: Cells that heal, not just chemicals that treat — living medicines.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of allogeneic cell therapies over autologous?
options: They use the patient's own cells, ensuring perfect compatibility
They are manufactured in advance from donor cells, available immediately off the shelf
They work only for blood cancers, not solid tumors

hook.text: Antibodies are great but bulky, expensive, and need cold storage — can we build something better?

buildup.text: DARPins are engineered repeat proteins — small, stable, and produced cheaply in bacteria.

discovery.text: Affibodies are 58 amino acids — they bind targets as tightly as antibodies but are 20 times smaller.

twist.text: Aptamers are not proteins at all — they are folded nucleic acids that bind targets like molecular origami.

climax.text: Abicipar, a DARPin for wet macular degeneration, lasted longer than ranibizumab — fewer injections needed.

punchline.text: Beyond antibodies — mimetics offer new shapes for old problems.

quiz.question: What advantage do antibody mimetics offer over traditional antibodies?
options: They always work better than antibodies in clinical trials
They are smaller, more stable, and cheaper to produce while binding targets with similar affinity
They do not require any regulatory approval before use

hook.text: A virus that kills cancer — oncolytic viruses infect tumor cells and burst them open while sparing healthy tissue.

buildup.text: Viruses are engineered to replicate only inside cancer cells — mutations disable their growth in normal tissue.

discovery.text: T-VEC is an approved herpes virus that destroys melanoma — it also releases signals that recruit the immune system.

twist.text: The immune system often clears the virus before it reaches distant tumors — delivery remains a major barrier.

climax.text: Combining oncolytic viruses with checkpoint inhibitors boosts response rates — the virus primes what immunotherapy finishes.

punchline.text: Fight fire with fire — oncolytic viruses turn infections into cancer cures.

quiz.question: How does T-VEC treat melanoma?
options: It blocks blood supply to melanoma tumors
It is an engineered herpes virus that selectively infects and destroys melanoma cells while stimulating immune response
It delivers chemotherapy drugs directly inside cancer cells

hook.text: Biopharmaceuticals are evolving fast — self-amplifying mRNA, encoded antibodies, and in vivo cell programming.

buildup.text: Self-amplifying mRNA replicates inside cells — a tiny dose produces the same protein as a large standard mRNA dose.

discovery.text: Encoded antibody therapy injects mRNA that instructs the body to make its own therapeutic antibodies — no factory needed.

twist.text: Oral biologics remain the holy grail — engineering proteins to survive stomach acid would end the injection era.

climax.text: AI designs biologics from scratch — generative models create antibodies that never existed in nature.

punchline.text: Living cells, smart molecules, AI design — biopharmaceuticals are just getting started.

quiz.question: What is encoded antibody therapy?
options: Injecting pre-made antibodies that encode information about the disease
Delivering mRNA that instructs the patient's own cells to produce therapeutic antibodies
Using AI to decode the structure of antibodies for manufacturing
